title: Converbs I: when, by, without
intro: A converb (*zarf-fiil*) turns a verb into an adverb: a clause that says when, how or in what order the main action happens. You know two already, `-(y)ken` and `-(y)Ip` from [A2 unit 11](gp-ken). This unit adds five: **when, once** `-(y)IncA`, **by, while** `-(y)ArAk`, **without** and **before** `-mAdAn`, **after** `-DIktAn sonra`, and **since** `-(y)AlI`. None of them takes a tense or a personal ending: the verb at the end of the sentence carries both.

blocks.text: `-(y)IncA` means **when** or **once**: the first action happens, and the second follows. *Eve gelince ararım* (When I get home, I'll call). Both of its vowels follow harmony, four-way on the first and two-way on the second: *-ınca, -ince, -unca, -ünce*. After a vowel it takes the buffer y (*okuyunca*), and the t of *git-* and *et-* becomes d before its vowel (*gidince*, *yardım edince*).

**No person, no tense.** *Gelince* is the same for **when I come**, **when she came** and **when they come**: the main verb says when, and the context who. *Eve gelince ararım* (When I get home, I'll call); *Eve gelince aradı* (When she got home, she called). The two parts can have different subjects, and then the first one is named: *Sen gelince başlarız* (We'll start when you come), *Otobüs gelince bindik* (When the bus came, we got on).

**A cause.** The first event often sets off the second, so `-(y)IncA` can carry a reason: *Yağmur başlayınca eve döndük* (When it started to rain, we went home). The negative, `-mAyIncA`, almost always does: *Otobüs gelmeyince yürüdük* (When the bus didn't come, we walked).
**With nouns and adjectives**, use *olunca*: *akşam olunca* (when evening comes), *hava güzel olunca* (when the weather is nice).

items.en: I'll call you when I get home.
When the lesson was over, we went to a café.
When it got dark, we went back home.
When the bus didn't come, we walked.
When evening came, we set off.

blocks.text: **Until.** Add the dative and *kadar* (until, [A2 unit 9](gp-postp-dative)): *Sen dönünceye kadar burada beklerim* (I'll wait here until you come back). The buffer y keeps the two vowels apart: *gelince-y-e*.

items.en: I'll wait here until you come back.

items.tr: Otobüs gelinceye kadar bir kafede oturduk.
items.seg: Otobüs gel|ince|y|e kadar bir kafede oturduk.
items.en: We sat in a café until the bus came.

blocks.title: Gelene kadar
blocks.text: In everyday speech, **until** is often *gelene kadar*, with the participle of [B1 unit 5](gp-participle-an): *Ben gelene kadar bekle* (Wait until I come). It means the same as *gelinceye kadar*; [B2 unit 10](gp-time-clauses) comes back to it.

blocks.title: While or once?
blocks.text: *Eve giderken ekmek aldım*: I bought bread **on the way** home, while still going. *Eve gidince yemek yaptım*: I cooked **once I was** home. `-ken` is for something in progress, `-(y)IncA` for something that has happened.
Write the softened stem and both harmonies: *gidince*, not *gitince*; *okuyunca*, not *okuyınca*. And *yiyince* but *deyince*: the TDK spelling keeps the e of *demek* here, as in *deyip*.

`-(y)ArAk` tells **how** something is done, or what else the subject is doing **at the same time**: *Koşarak geldi* (She came running), *Müzik dinleyerek ders çalışıyorum* (I study while listening to music). It has two-way harmony (*-arak*, *-erek*), the buffer y after a vowel (*okuyarak*, *bekleyerek*), and the softened t of *git-* and *et-* (*giderek*, *yardım ederek*). *Yemek* and *demek* write an i: *yiyerek*, *diyerek*.

blocks.caption: `-(y)ArAk` on common verbs
head: Verb
Converb
Example
rows: *İşe yürüyerek gidiyorum.* I walk to work.
*Gülerek cevap verdi.* He answered with a laugh.
*Müzik dinleyerek çalışırım.* I work with music on.
*Çok çalışarak kazandı.* She won by working hard.
*Simit yiyerek yürüyordu.* He was walking along, eating a simit.

blocks.text: **The same subject.** Whoever does the `-(y)ArAk` action is the subject of the main verb: *Ayşe gülerek konuştu* (Ayşe spoke, laughing). For two different people, use `-ken`: *Ben konuşurken Ayşe güldü* (Ayşe laughed while I was talking).

**By doing.** `-(y)ArAk` also gives the means: *Çok çalışarak sınavı geçti* (She passed the exam by working hard), *Bu kelimeleri şarkı dinleyerek öğrendim* (I learned these words by listening to songs).

**Words in their own right.** A few `-(y)ArAk` forms have become words. *Olarak* (being) means **as**: *Öğretmen olarak çalışıyor* (She works as a teacher), *ilk olarak* (first of all), *genel olarak* (in general). *Giderek* (going) means **more and more, gradually**: *Şehir giderek büyüyor* (The city keeps growing). *Severek* means **gladly**: *Severek yardım ederim* (I'd be glad to help).

items.en: The children ran out into the garden.
She answered with a laugh.
I study while listening to music.
I spent the holiday reading books.
My mother works as a teacher.

blocks.title: Two steps or one?
blocks.text: `-Ip` ([A2 unit 11](gp-ip)) links two steps, one after the other: *Eve koşup çantamı aldım* (I ran home and got my bag). `-(y)ArAk` describes one action and how it was done: *Eve koşarak geldim* (I came home running).
French en + present participle often says the same: en courant is *koşarak*, en écoutant de la musique is *müzik dinleyerek*.
**Without doing** is not the negative of `-(y)ArAk`. *Bakmayarak* exists but is rare; say *bakmadan*, as the next section explains.

sections.title: Bakmadan, yatmadan önce: -mAdAn, without and before

blocks.text: `-mAdAn` (*-madan*, *-meden*) means **without doing**: *Kahvaltı yapmadan çıktım* (I left without having breakfast), *Hiçbir şey söylemeden gitti* (He left without saying anything). It begins with the negative `-mA`, so no stem ever changes: *gitmeden*, *yemeden*, *demeden*.

**Before.** With *önce* after it, `-mAdAn` means **before**: *Yatmadan önce kitap okurum* (I read before going to bed). Nothing is denied, even though the form looks negative: you do go to bed, after the book. Even without *önce*, `-mAdAn` often means **before** when the main action is meant to come first: *Hava kararmadan dönelim* (Let's go back before it gets dark).

**Subjects and orders.** The first part can have its own subject: *Sen gelmeden başlamayız* (We won't start before you come, or without you). And the main verb can be an order: *Bakmadan karşıya geçme!* (Don't cross without looking!)

items.en: I left without having breakfast; I'm starving.
He left without saying anything.
I read before going to bed.

items.tr: Evden çıkmadan önce pasaportunu kontrol et.
items.seg: Evden çık|ma|dan önce pasaportunu kontrol et.
items.en: Check your passport before you leave home.
Let's go back before it gets dark.

blocks.title: Before a noun, before a verb
blocks.text: With a noun, **before** is the ablative + *önce*: *yemekten önce* (before the meal, [A2 unit 9](gp-postp-ablative)). With a verb, it is `-mAdAn önce`: *yemek yemeden önce* (before eating). There is no *-DIktAn önce*.
Formal writing has another **without**, `-mAksIzIn` (*beklemeksizin*, without waiting). It comes in [B2 unit 3](gp-maksizin).

**After** an action is the `-DIk` of [B1 unit 6](gp-participle-dik), without a possessive, plus the ablative and *sonra*: *ye-dik-ten sonra* (after eating). Both D's become t after a voiceless consonant (*gittikten*, *yaptıktan*), and harmony gives *-dıktan, -dikten, -duktan, -dükten*. The stem never changes: *gittikten*, *yedikten*.

With nouns, you know *yemekten sonra* (after the meal). With verbs, use `-DIktAn sonra`: *yemek yedikten sonra* (after eating). As with the other converbs, the subjects can differ: *Sen gittikten sonra Ali geldi* (Ali came after you left).
**How long after.** Put the time span before *sonra*: *Mezun olduktan iki yıl sonra evlendi* (She got married two years after graduating).

**-DIktAn sonra or -(y)IncA?** Both put one event after another. `-DIktAn sonra` is a plain **after**. `-(y)IncA` is **once, as soon as**, and often hints that one thing led to the other: *Haberi duyunca çok sevindi* (She was delighted when she heard the news).

items.en: After eating, we went for a walk.

items.tr: Üniversiteden mezun olduktan sonra İzmir'e taşındı.
items.seg: Üniversiteden mezun ol|duk|tan sonra İzmir'e taşındı.
items.en: After graduating from university, she moved to Izmir.
Ali came after you left.
After they retired, they moved to the village.

items.tr: Türkiye'ye geldikten iki yıl sonra evlendi.
items.seg: Türkiye'ye gel|dik|ten iki yıl sonra evlendi.
items.en: He got married two years after coming to Turkey.

blocks.text: **Before** and **after** are built differently: `-mAdAn önce` but `-DIktAn sonra`. *Gittikten önce* and *gitmeden sonra* don't exist.

`-(y)AlI` counts the time **since** an event. It has two-way harmony (*-alı*, *-eli*) and the buffer y after a vowel (*başlayalı*), and it usually comes with a time span and *oldu* (it has been): *Buraya geleli üç yıl oldu* (It's been three years since I came here), *Ali gideli iki saat oldu* (Ali left two hours ago; literally, it's been two hours since Ali left).

head: Verb
Converb
Example
rows: *Buraya geleli üç yıl oldu.* It's been three years since I came here.
*Evleneli on yıl oldu.* We've been married for ten years.
*Türkçeye başlayalı bir yıl oldu.* I started Turkish a year ago.
*Taşınalı bir ay olmadı.* We moved here less than a month ago.
*Seni görmeyeli çok oldu.* I haven't seen you for ages.

blocks.text: **The negative**, `-mAyAlI`, counts from the last time something happened, which English says the other way round: *Seni görmeyeli çok oldu* (I haven't seen you for ages; literally, since not seeing you, it has been long). *Görüşmeyeli çok oldu!* is the everyday **Long time no see!**

**Questions** use *ne kadar*: *Buraya geleli ne kadar oldu?* (How long is it since you came here?). Without a time span, `-(y)AlI` can also mean **ever since**: *Bu eve taşınalı çok mutluyuz* (We've been very happy since we moved into this house).

**-(y)AlI or -DIr?** `-DIr` ([A2 unit 9](gp-duration-dir)) measures a state that is still going on: *Üç yıldır buradayım* (I've been here for three years). `-(y)AlI` counts from one event: *Buraya geleli üç yıl oldu*. Often both fit: *On yıldır evliyiz* or *Evleneli on yıl oldu*.

items.en: It's been three years since I came here.
Ali left two hours ago.

items.tr: Türkçe öğrenmeye başlayalı bir yıl oldu.
items.seg: Türkçe öğrenmeye başla|y|alı bir yıl oldu.
items.en: It's been a year since I started learning Turkish.
Long time no see!
My mother has been very happy since she retired.

blocks.text: `-(y)AlI` has two-way harmony, like `-(y)ArAk`: *geleli*, *başlayalı*, never *gelili*. And *git-* softens before it: *gideli*.

summary: Converbs take no tense and no person: the main verb at the end gives both, and the converb clause can have its own subject (*Sen gelince başlarız*).
`-(y)IncA` is **when, once**: *Eve gelince ararım*; negative *gelmeyince*; on nouns *olunca*. **Until** is `-(y)IncAyA kadar`: *dönünceye kadar*.
`-(y)ArAk` is **by** or **while**, with the same subject: *Koşarak geldi*, *Müzik dinleyerek çalışıyorum*; also *olarak* (as), *giderek* (more and more), *severek* (gladly).
`-mAdAn` is **without**: *Kahvaltı yapmadan çıktım*; with *önce*, **before**: *Yatmadan önce kitap okurum*.
`-DIktAn sonra` is **after**: *yedikten sonra*, *mezun olduktan iki yıl sonra*.
`-(y)AlI` + a time span + *oldu* is **it's been … since**: *Buraya geleli üç yıl oldu*, *Görüşmeyeli çok oldu!*
Spelling: *gidince, giderek, gideli*; *yiyince, yiyerek*, but *deyince* and *diyerek*.
